name: Family Dinner Chaos
blurb: An honest Sunday dinner, five family members, and five secrets that fall out one by one
title: Family Dinner Chaos: Funny Skit Script for 5 People
description: A 5-minute comedy skit script for 5: at an honest family dinner, everyone hides a secret and they come out one by one. Free to perform and film.
h1: Family Dinner Chaos: a 5-Minute Comedy Skit Script for 5 People
logline: Gran makes a new rule for Sunday dinner: no phones, no secrets. The trouble is that every person at the table is hiding something, and each confession pulls the next one out, until the biggest secret of all rings the doorbell.
setting: A family dining table. Props: a table and five chairs, plates and forks, a covered dish (any dish with a lid or a tea towel over it), an apron, napkins, a watch.

roles.name: Dad
roles.note: Adult. Proud of his lasagne, which he did not make.

roles.name: Mum
roles.note: Adult. Sensible, caring, and humming a piano tune for six months.

roles.name: Gran
roles.note: Older adult. The boss of the table. Made the honesty rule for a reason.

roles.name: Rio
roles.note: Teen, any gender. Supposed to be at piano lessons. Secretly an excellent cook.

roles.name: Kit
roles.note: Younger child, any gender (any age actor). First to crack, and loving it.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – A family dining table, Sunday evening

script.action: A table with five chairs, plates and a big covered dish in the middle. DAD stands proudly beside it in an apron. MUM, GRAN, RIO and KIT sit down.

script.say: Ladies and gentlemen. My homemade lasagne. Four hours of work.

script.action: Dad lifts the cover. Everyone applauds.

script.say: Before we eat, a family rule. Sunday dinner is honest dinner. No phones. No secrets.

script.action: Everyone nods a little too fast.

script.say: Of course. No secrets.
Never.
Who has secrets? Not this family.

script.action: Kit drops a spoon. Kit bends under the table for a long time.

script.say: Kit, what are you doing down there?
Nothing. Looking for the spoon. And something else.
What else?
Honest dinner?
Honest dinner.
I lost the spare house key. On Monday. I've been climbing in through the kitchen window all week.
The window? That's why the plant is always on the floor!
The plant knows. The plant has always known.
Kit! That's dangerous.
I feel amazing. Can I have the biggest piece?
One secret out. Lovely. Who's next?

script.action: Silence. Rio takes a bite of lasagne. Chews. Frowns. Chews again.

script.say: Dad. This has fresh basil, a three-cheese sauce and a little nutmeg.
Yes. My special recipe.
This is the number six from the little restaurant by the station.

script.action: Everyone stops chewing and looks at Dad.

script.say: How... how would you know that?
Because I've cooked it. Twenty times.
You cook? Since when?
Since I stopped going to piano lessons. Six months ago. Tuesday evenings, I go to the cooking club at the community centre instead.
Six months? We've been paying for piano!
I know. I'm sorry. I really, really hate the piano.
And you, chef?
The oven broke on Wednesday. I panicked. I ordered it. I hid the boxes in the car. I put flour on my face for the photo.
There's a photo?
I sent it to my brother. He said I look like a real chef.
Three secrets. This is the best Sunday in years.

script.action: Everyone turns to Mum. Mum is looking at the ceiling.

script.say: What?
Mum.
I don't have a secret.
You're humming.
Am I?
You've been humming the same piano tune for six months.
Fine. Rio, I know you skip piano.
You knew?
The teacher called me in the first week. She said the lessons were already paid for the whole year. It seemed like such a waste.
So?
So I go. Tuesday evenings. I'm actually very good. I can play the little song with both hands.
You've been taking MY piano lessons?
And you've been not taking them. It's teamwork.

script.action: Everyone laughs. Then they all slowly turn to Gran, who is eating calmly.

script.say: Lovely lasagne, whoever made it.
Gran. Honest dinner.
I made the rule. The rule is for you.
Mum!
Fine. I've been seeing someone.
Seeing someone? Like a doctor?
Like a gentleman. His name is Harold. We met three weeks ago. He has lovely manners and a very fast scooter.
A scooter?
He's coming to meet you all tonight. That's why I made the rule. I wanted everything honest before he arrived.
Tonight? When?
About now.
That's probably the dessert. I ordered tiramisu. From the same restaurant.
Oh, I know. That's Harold.
What?
He delivers for the restaurant by the station. He told me a man on our street orders lasagne every Sunday and puts flour on his face.

script.action: Everyone looks at Dad. Dad slowly puts the apron back on.

script.say: Nobody open the door.
I'll go through the window.

script.action: Gran stands, fixes her hair, and walks to the door with great dignity. Everyone else hides behind their napkins. Blackout.

ul: Set the table side-on to the audience, with chairs only on the back and the two short ends, so nobody has their back to the room. Gran sits at one end like a judge.
The covered dish is the centre of the stage. Lift the cover with a big gesture at the start; it is the lie the whole skit is built on.
Each confession should change the table: the confessor relaxes and eats, the others lean in. By the end only Gran is calm.
The doorbell can be a student offstage saying ding-dong, a phone sound, or a knock. Use it twice, the second one louder.
Land the ending with movement: Gran rises slowly and walks off with dignity while everyone else lifts their napkins to hide their faces in one move.
The game is a chain: each secret is discovered because of the one before it. Make the links clear by turning heads together to the next person.
Confessions are a relief, not a tragedy. Each person should look lighter after they confess, which pushes the others to crack.
Rio's food analysis is a sudden expert moment. Slow, serious, like a judge on a cooking show. Then the line about the restaurant hits fast.
Mum's humming should start quietly early in the scene so the audience half-notices it before Kit points it out.
Gran's reveal about Harold needs no rush. She enjoys every second. The faster everyone else panics, the slower Gran should be.
Common mistake: everyone talking at once after each reveal. Pick one reaction line, then silence, then move on.
Change the occasion to a holiday or a birthday dinner your audience knows, and change the dish to a local favourite that is easy to order in.
For a cast of six, add an uncle or older sibling with a secret of their own, for example they have secretly been the one watering the window plant.
Part-two hook: the door opens and Harold walks in carrying tiramisu and a small velvet box for Gran.

prompts.keyframe: A family of five at a dinner table, a proud father in an apron lifting the lid off a dish, a grandmother at the head of the table, warm evening home lighting, wide shot, cinematic still, 16:9
shots: Medium shot, slow push in on a teenager chewing food with a suspicious frown while the family watches nervously, warm dinner light, comedic tension
Wide shot, the whole family slowly turns their heads toward a calm grandmother eating, then jumps as a doorbell rings, comedic surprise
Static wide shot, a grandmother walks proudly toward a front door while the rest of the family hides behind napkins at the table, playful ending

faq.q: Can we perform Family Dinner Chaos at a school event or film it for a channel?
faq.a: Yes. It is free to perform and film under CC BY 4.0, including monetised videos and competitions. Credit "Script: cv.cm".

faq.q: Do Dad, Mum and Gran have to be played by adults?
faq.a: No. Students can play every role; a jacket, glasses or a cardigan is enough. You can also swap them to Grandpa, an aunt or an older cousin, as long as Gran's role stays the calm boss of the table.

faq.q: How long does it run and how should we rehearse the chain of secrets?
faq.a: About five minutes. Rehearse it in five small blocks, one per secret, then run the joins. Each block ends with everyone turning to the next person; that head-turn is the cue that keeps the pace.
